runs.t: Few animals rearrange the land around them as thoroughly as the beaver. There are two living species, the Eurasian beaver and the North American beaver, and both are heavy, slow-moving, semi-aquatic rodents that spend their lives at the edge of fresh water. Only the capybara of South America is a larger rodent. For most of the twentieth century the beaver was, in Europe at least, a curiosity. Trapped for centuries, it clung on in a few isolated populations along remote rivers, and in Britain it had been absent for some four hundred years. Today the animal is back across much of its former range, and with it has come a long argument about what a river is for.

A beaver is built for a life divided between water and wood. Its hind feet are webbed for swimming. The broad, flattened tail, covered in scales, works as a rudder and as a prop when the animal sits back to gnaw; slapped hard on the surface, it also warns the rest of the family that a predator is near. The coat has two layers: long outer hairs and, beneath them, a dense underfur that traps air and keeps the skin dry. Underwater, a transparent membrane slides across each eye like a pair of goggles, and the nostrils and ears close. Most useful of all, the lips meet behind the front teeth, so a beaver can cut and carry wood while submerged without taking in water. Those front teeth, or incisors, never stop growing, and because the enamel on their outer face is strengthened with iron they are both unusually hard and distinctly orange.

Not every beaver builds a dam. Where a river is already deep and steady, a family will simply dig a burrow into the bank. Dams are a response to shallow water, and the trigger seems to be sound: a beaver that hears running water will pile branches, stones and mud against the noise until it stops. The pond that forms behind the dam has one essential function, which is to stay deep enough that it does not freeze to the bottom in winter. In the middle of it the family builds a lodge of sticks plastered with mud, with sleeping chambers above the waterline and every entrance below it, so that no fox or wolf can walk in. Through the autumn the animals push cut branches into the mud near the lodge, building a larder that can be reached from underneath the ice. A colony is usually a single pair with their young of the last two seasons.

The consequences for the valley are out of all proportion to the size of the animal. Water held behind a dam spreads sideways instead of rushing downstream, and as it slows it drops the silt it was carrying. The water table rises, so the surrounding ground stays damp late into a dry summer. Trees standing in the new pond die and remain upright for years, and this standing dead wood is used by woodpeckers, by beetles and by the birds that hunt them. The shallow margins fill with frogs, dragonflies and young fish. In time a single stream can become a staircase of ponds, pools and side channels. When a colony moves on and the dam finally fails, the pond drains and its deep bed of silt is colonised by grasses and flowers, producing the open, damp clearing that North American naturalists call a beaver meadow.

It was fur that nearly ended all this. Beaver underfur can be matted into an excellent felt, and for two centuries the hats made from that felt were the uniform of respectable Europe. The animal was also hunted for castoreum, a pungent secretion from glands near the tail, which was burned as incense and sold by apothecaries as a remedy for headache and fever. Trapping alone might not have been fatal, but it was combined with the steady drainage of marshes for farmland and the removal of dams and fallen timber to make rivers passable for boats and mills. By the start of the twentieth century the Eurasian beaver survived only in scattered pockets in France, Germany, Norway and the east of the continent.

Recovery, when it came, was rapid, and it has not been painless. Beavers do not distinguish between a willow and an orchard, and a dam placed in the wrong ditch will flood a field of barley or block the culvert under a road. Much of the practical work of the last thirty years has therefore been about living alongside a rodent rather than merely releasing one. Valuable trees can be wrapped in wire mesh or painted with a gritty mixture that is unpleasant to gnaw. A pipe laid through a dam, with its inlet set well upstream of the structure, drains the pond quietly to a chosen level without alerting the builders, who hear nothing and so repair nothing. Where such measures fail, licences allow dams to be removed. The wider case for tolerance is an economic one: a chain of beaver ponds holds back water in a flood, releases it in a drought, and filters out the soil and fertiliser that would otherwise end up in the reservoir downstream. Whether that service is worth the barley is now a question for policy rather than for natural history.

runs.t: How the railway and the telegraph persuaded the world to abandon its own local hour.

For almost all of recorded history, time was a local matter. Noon was the moment at which the sun stood highest over a particular town, and since the sun reaches different places at different moments, every town kept an hour of its own. Bristol was roughly ten minutes behind London; a traveller moving west across England was, in effect, moving slowly backwards through the morning. Nobody was inconvenienced by this. A journey by coach took so long, and was so uncertain, that a discrepancy of a few minutes between one church clock and the next was invisible. Appointments were made for the morning or the afternoon rather than for the half-hour, and the working day was measured by daylight and by the bell.

The railway destroyed that comfortable vagueness within a generation. A train could cross the distance between two towns faster than the difference between their clocks, which produced timetables that appeared to describe arrivals before departures. More seriously, much early track was single, with trains passing one another at agreed places and agreed moments; if the two drivers were working to clocks set in different towns, the agreement was worthless. Passengers missed connections, and inspectors investigating collisions found that they could not establish the order in which events had happened. Speed had turned a harmless irregularity into a hazard, and the companies, rather than any government, were the first to act on it.

What made a shared hour practical was not the railway but the electric telegraph, which carried a signal from one end of a country to the other in a moment. Time could now be sent as well as kept. The Royal Observatory at Greenwich had long dropped a large ball down a mast at one o’clock each afternoon so that ships in the river could check their chronometers before sailing, but a time ball can only be seen from a few miles away. Once observatories were wired to the telegraph network they could distribute a signal daily to stations, post offices and jewellers along the line, and the jewellers in turn corrected the watches of the town. An accurate hour had become something that could be transmitted, bought and sold.

Through the 1840s the British railway companies adopted a single standard, Greenwich time, across their networks, and by the middle of the century most public clocks in the country followed them. The change was not universally welcomed. To set a clock by an observatory two hundred miles away was to accept that a distant institution now defined when a local day began and ended, and some towns kept both hours going at once, with a second minute hand painted on the dial of the town clock. There was also a legal muddle, because the law still recognised local time: a document signed, a licence expiring or a poll closing at a stated hour could fall on either side of a deadline depending on which clock was consulted. Parliament did not confirm Greenwich time as the legal time of Great Britain until 1880, forty years after the railways had settled the matter in practice.

North America faced the same problem on a far larger scale. Its railroads ran on dozens of different company times, and a large interchange station might display half a dozen clocks, one for each line using the platforms. In 1883 the railroads themselves agreed to divide the continent into a small number of broad belts, within each of which every clock would show the same hour, with a jump of exactly sixty minutes at each boundary. Again the industry moved first: the change was introduced by private agreement, and the government of the United States did not give the arrangement the force of law for another thirty-five years.

A continent could organise itself, but a world could not do so without agreeing where to begin counting. Charts and almanacs measured longitude from a variety of starting lines, and a system of hourly zones is meaningless unless everyone uses the same one. The Canadian railway engineer Sandford Fleming argued through the 1870s and 1880s for a single global scheme of standard hours reckoned from one meridian. At a conference held in Washington in 1884, delegates from a large number of countries recommended that the meridian passing through Greenwich should be adopted as the common zero, a decision that owed less to astronomy than to the fact that most of the world’s shipping already carried British charts. The recommendation bound nobody, and adoption took decades; several countries kept their own meridian for years afterwards, and a few regions chose offsets of half an hour rather than a whole one, as some still do.

The result was a quiet revolution in everyday discipline. Once an authoritative hour was available to everyone, it could be used to govern not only trains but shifts, school lessons, market openings and the working day itself, and lateness became a measurable offence rather than a matter of opinion. The modern descendants of the time ball are the signals that synchronise computer networks and satellites, accurate now to fractions of a second, but the principle is unchanged: somewhere a clock is defined as correct, and everybody else agrees to follow it. It is worth remembering that the hour shown on a phone is not a fact about the sun. It is an administrative convenience, invented for the convenience of traffic, and the sun over most towns is no longer overhead at noon.

title.t: Does the Language We Speak Shape the Way We Think?

runs.t: The idea that a language quietly organises the minds of the people who speak it is one of the most attractive propositions in the human sciences, and one of the most frequently abused. In its strong form, associated with the American linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, it holds that the categories of a language determine the categories of thought, so that speakers of very different languages inhabit, in some meaningful sense, different worlds. In its weak form it claims only that the distinctions a language obliges its speakers to make will, through sheer repetition, become the distinctions they attend to most readily. The strong version was largely abandoned by the middle of the twentieth century. The weak version, after thirty years of more careful experiment, is in better health, and it is worth being clear about why the first failed and what exactly the second has established.

The strong claim collapsed partly on the evidence and partly on logic. Whorf’s best-known argument, that one North American language lacked the means to express time as Europeans understood it, rested on an analysis that later specialists in that language rejected. A second favourite illustration, the supposed abundance of words for snow in Arctic languages, turned out to depend entirely on how one decides to count words in a language that builds long words out of small parts; by the same method English has indefinitely many words for anything. The logical difficulty is more serious. If the limits of a language really were the limits of thought, no speaker could ever acquire an idea that the language did not already encode, and the history of every technical vocabulary shows that they do. A language that lacks a single word for an idea can always reach it with a phrase, which is why translation is laborious rather than impossible.

What revived the field was a shift from grand claims about world views to small claims that could be tested. The most convincing results concern space. Most European languages describe the position of objects relative to the body: the cup is to my left, the church is in front of me. A number of languages, including some spoken in northern Australia and in southern Mexico, do not offer this option for most purposes and require instead a fixed, geographic frame: the cup is to the north of the plate, whichever way the speaker happens to be facing. Speakers of such languages perform a remarkable feat of continuous reckoning, remaining correctly oriented indoors, in unfamiliar towns and after being turned around, because nothing they say about position can be formulated without it. Asked to arrange a sequence of pictures in order, they tend to lay them out along a fixed compass line rather than from their own left to their own right. Here a grammatical obligation plainly trains an everyday skill, and the writer regards this as the strongest evidence in the whole debate.

Colour has produced a subtler result. Languages carve the spectrum differently, and some treat lighter and darker blue as two basic colours rather than as shades of one. Speakers of those languages are measurably quicker to tell the two blues apart than speakers of languages that use a single term. That looks like perception shaped by vocabulary, until the experiment is repeated while the participants are made to hold a string of words in memory, an arrangement that occupies the language system and leaves the eyes alone. The advantage then disappears. The natural reading is not that these speakers see different colours but that, in a task requiring a rapid decision, they silently recruit a verbal label that other speakers do not have available. Language is behaving less like a lens through which the world is perceived and more like a tool picked up when it happens to be useful.

Grammatical gender has been a more troublesome case. Many languages assign nouns to classes marked on articles and adjectives, and a well-publicised line of research reported that speakers describe the same object with different adjectives depending on the gender its name carries in their language, choosing words such as
sturdy
where the noun is masculine and
elegant

where it is feminine. The effects, where they appear, are small, several attempts to reproduce them have failed, and critics have pointed out that such studies have often been conducted with bilingual participants responding in English, so that whatever is measured may belong to the act of translation rather than to the original language. The honest summary is that the question remains open.

Claims made outside the laboratory deserve more scepticism still. It has been argued, on the basis of statistics covering many countries, that speakers of languages which oblige them to mark the future tense grammatically save less money and take worse care of their health, on the grounds that such grammar makes the future feel remote. The correlation is real, but a language is not an isolated variable: the nations grouped together by this feature also share histories, religions, institutions and climates, any of which might explain the difference. Worse, languages are related by descent, so a sample of hundreds of languages may contain only a handful of genuinely independent cases, and a statistical test that treats each language as a separate observation will report a confidence it has not earned. Correlations of this kind are a prompt for investigation, not a finding.

What survives, then, is a modest and rather interesting conclusion. Speaking a language requires a speaker to attend, constantly and automatically, to whatever that language forces them to specify, and this habit of attention leaves traces in memory, in classification and in the direction of a casual glance. It does not install a different reality. The effects are real, they are measurable, and they are small, which is precisely why they are so regularly misreported: a result about reaction times becomes, by the time it reaches a newspaper, a claim that some people cannot perceive the colour blue. Readers would be wise to treat any headline announcing that a language makes its speakers unable to grasp something as a translation error of its own.

A coral reef looks like rock, and in a sense it is, but it is rock made by animals. The builder is the coral polyp, a small, soft-bodied creature that is little more than a column of tissue crowned with a ring of stinging tentacles. Polyps are relatives of the sea anemones and the jellyfish, and like them they catch food by stinging it. What makes the reef-building corals different is a chemical habit: they take calcium and carbonate from the surrounding seawater and lay them down as limestone underneath themselves, so that each animal sits in a small stony cup of its own making. A polyp divides to produce another polyp, which does the same, and the result is a colony of thousands of genetically identical individuals sharing a single skeleton. Successive generations build on the skeletons of those that came before, and a reef is simply that accumulation, continued for thousands of years. The process is slow. The fastest branching corals add a few centimetres in a year, and the massive, boulder-shaped species far less than that, which is why damage done in an afternoon can take a century to repair.

The polyp does not work alone. Inside the tissues of every reef-building coral there live enormous numbers of single-celled algae. They are sheltered there, and they are supplied with the waste products of their host, which to a plant are valuable nutrients. In return they photosynthesise, and they pass a large share of the sugars they make to the coral around them. For a coral growing in clear, sunlit water, this internal garden provides most of the energy it needs; the tentacles, which are put out mainly at night to catch drifting plankton, supply the remainder. The algae also account for the appearance of the reef. Coral tissue is itself almost colourless, and the browns, golds and greens of a healthy colony are the colours of the crop it carries. The partnership is what allows corals to grow fast enough to build a structure that the sea is constantly trying to pull down.

It also explains where reefs can and cannot grow. Because the algae need light, reef-building corals are confined to shallow water, and because they need warmth they are found mostly in a broad belt either side of the equator. They require a firm foundation to settle on, and clear water, since suspended sediment both shuts out the light and settles on the polyps, which must then spend energy cleaning themselves. These conditions are met in the open tropical ocean, and the open tropical ocean is one of the least productive environments on earth, so poor in dissolved nutrients that it is often described as a marine desert. The reef sits in the middle of this desert and supports a quantity of life that is out of all proportion to its surroundings: a small fraction of one per cent of the sea floor shelters something approaching a quarter of all marine species. The explanation lies in the partnership. Nutrients that elsewhere would sink into deep water are passed back and forth within the reef instead of being lost, and very little is wasted.

That dependence has a cost. When a coral is placed under stress it expels the algae from its tissues, sometimes within a few days. Since the tissue is transparent and the algae are gone, what the eye now sees is the white limestone skeleton beneath, and the colony is said to have bleached. A bleached coral has not died. It has lost the greater part of its food supply, and it is starving. If the stress passes quickly, algae recolonise the tissue over the following weeks or months and the colony regains both its colour and its growth, although it may not reproduce that year. If the stress continues, the coral starves, and the skeleton is soon colonised by seaweeds and worn away by the many organisms that bore into it.

A number of things can cause bleaching. Very low tides that leave corals exposed to the air will do it, as will sudden floods of fresh water after heavy rain, a heavy load of sediment washed off the land, certain pollutants, and even an unusual cold spell. By far the most important cause, however, is water that is unusually warm for that place and that season. Corals live close to their upper limit for much of the year, and a rise of only a degree or two above the normal summer maximum, held for several weeks, is enough to break the partnership. The distinction matters, because the local causes affect a bay or a stretch of shore, while abnormally warm water can settle over an entire sea for a whole summer and bleach reefs across thousands of kilometres at once.

When a reef dies, the loss is structural as well as biological. The limestone remains, but nothing is adding to it, and the agents of destruction do not pause: boring sponges and molluscs weaken it from within, grazing fish and urchins scrape at it from without, and storms break up what is left. Within a few years an intricate landscape of branches, overhangs and crevices has been reduced to rubble and a low pavement. The animals that depended on those hiding places go with them, and the fisheries that support many coastal communities decline. Reefs also provide coastal protection, absorbing much of the energy of waves before it reaches the shore, and a flattened reef absorbs far less, so that beaches erode and low-lying land floods more readily than it did. Tourism, which in some countries is a significant part of the national income, suffers in its turn.

None of this makes the situation hopeless, and a good deal can be done locally. Reducing the sewage, fertiliser and soil that run off the land removes one source of stress and gives a reef a better chance of recovering from another. Protecting the fish that graze on seaweed matters more than it sounds, because after a coral dies the contest for the bare space is between young corals and fast-growing algae, and where grazers have been fished out the algae win. Restoration adds to this: fragments of coral are grown in underwater nurseries on frames suspended above the sea bed, and are later planted on damaged reefs, while researchers are working with colonies that have survived repeated heat and attempting to breed from them. Such work is valuable, but nobody involved in it claims more than that it buys time. A reef can be defended against pollution, against overfishing and against careless anchoring by the people who live beside it; it cannot be defended by them against the temperature of the ocean.

runs.t: The bicycle took eighty years to arrive at a shape it has barely altered since.

There is nothing in a bicycle that could not, in principle, have been made in the ancient world, and yet the machine is barely two hundred years old. The delay is usually explained by metal. A bicycle depends on parts that are light, accurately round and accurately matched — bearings, a chain, thin tubes, wire spokes under tension — and such parts only became cheap once industry could roll, draw and cut steel in quantity. The history of the bicycle is therefore less a story of a single inventor than a story of a series of workshops solving one problem at a time, each solution creating the next difficulty.

The ancestor of all of them appeared in Germany in 1817, when Karl von Drais built a wooden running machine: two wheels in line, a padded saddle on a beam between them, and a front wheel that could be steered. It had no pedals, and the rider propelled it by pushing against the ground with the feet, in long strides, lifting them when the machine ran downhill. It looks today like a toy, but it settled the question on which everything later depended, which is that a two-wheeled vehicle does not fall over while it is moving and can be balanced by steering. For two or three seasons it was fashionable in London and Paris. Then the fashion passed, not least because riders took to the pavements, where they frightened pedestrians and were promptly banned, and the roads of the day were too rough and too muddy to be enjoyable.

The next step waited half a century. In Paris in the 1860s a workshop fitted cranks and pedals directly to the axle of the front wheel, so that the rider could drive the machine without touching the ground. The result was called a velocipede, and in English, with feeling, the boneshaker. Its wheels were wooden with iron tyres, its frame had no springing to speak of, and the streets were cobbled; the name was earned. All the same it was the first bicycle to be manufactured in large numbers, it was exported across Europe and to America, and it produced the first racing clubs and the first road races. It also exposed a problem. Because the pedals turned the wheel directly, one turn of the rider's legs carried the machine forward by exactly the circumference of that wheel, and no faster.

The answer was to make the wheel enormous. Through the 1870s the driven front wheel grew until it was as large as the rider's legs could straddle, while the trailing wheel shrank to little more than a stabiliser, producing the high bicycle, later nicknamed the penny-farthing. These machines were a real advance in engineering. Their wheels were built on the modern principle, with thin wire spokes carrying the load in tension rather than thick wooden ones carrying it in compression, and they ran on solid rubber tyres, so the high bicycle was both faster and lighter than anything before it. It was also alarming. The rider sat almost directly above the axle of a wheel five feet across, with his weight high and well forward, and if that wheel struck a stone or a rut the machine stopped and he did not, but was pitched over the handlebars head first. Falls of this kind were common enough to have a name of their own. The high bicycle remained, inevitably, a machine for athletic young men with money.

What replaced it was the safety bicycle, which took shape in English workshops in the 1880s and reached its familiar form in Starley's Rover of 1885. Its central idea was indirect drive: a chain running from a pedalled sprocket to a smaller sprocket on the rear wheel, so that one turn of the pedals produced more than one turn of the wheel. Gearing had separated speed from wheel size. The wheels could now be equal, and modest, the rider could sit low between them with his feet within reach of the ground, and the frame settled into the familiar arrangement of triangles that gives the greatest stiffness for the least weight. The last piece arrived in 1888 with the pneumatic tyre, a tube of air inside a rubber casing, which made riding far more comfortable on rough surfaces and, to everyone's surprise, faster as well, because a tyre that absorbs a bump wastes less of the rider's effort than a rigid one that is thrown into the air by it. The idea had in fact been patented decades earlier and forgotten.

The 1890s were the result: a boom in which bicycles were bought in millions, and then, as the new machines passed into second-hand hands, a change in who could travel. A working man could reach employment ten miles from his village. A woman could leave her own street unaccompanied, which is why the bicycle appears so often in the arguments of the period about what women might wear and where they might go; the heavy skirts of the day were impossible on a machine, and the dress reformers made the point loudly. The industry mattered too. Firms that had learned to make ball bearings, light steel tubing, chains and wheels in quantity were precisely the firms that went on to build motor cars and, in more than one famous case, aircraft. Cyclists had meanwhile organised themselves and begun to campaign for smoother road surfaces, well before the motorist existed to benefit from them.

After about 1910 the bicycle lost its glamour in the wealthier countries and became, for fifty years, the transport of those who could not yet afford a car, while in much of the rest of the world it simply remained the way people got about. Its recent revival in European cities has less to do with nostalgia than with arithmetic: measured as energy spent per person per kilometre, a cyclist is the most efficient traveller on earth, more efficient than any machine and than any walking or swimming animal. It is a curious kind of success. Almost everything else built in 1890 has been superseded, but the bicycle in a modern shop is recognisably the safety bicycle, improved in its materials and barely altered in its plan.

title.t: Room to Breathe: Green Space and the Health of Cities

runs.t: That parks are good for us has become one of those propositions that nobody in urban policy troubles to argue for any more. It appears in planning documents, in the prospectuses of property developers and in the speeches of mayors, generally in a form broad enough to be unfalsifiable. The proposition is, in the main, true; what is rarely acknowledged is that it covers several quite different claims, supported by evidence of very unequal quality, and that the differences between them have consequences for how a city spends a limited budget. A claim that trees reduce the temperature of a street in a heatwave is of a different order from a claim that a park improves the mental health of the people who live near it, and both differ from a claim that planting one will make a neighbourhood more equal.

The starting point is a very large body of population research, gathered in many countries, which consistently finds that people living in greener neighbourhoods report better mental health, show lower levels of stress hormones and suffer less cardiovascular disease than people living in less green ones, and that these differences survive statistical adjustment for income and education. The consistency is impressive. The difficulty is that almost all of this work is observational, and observational data cannot establish which way the causation runs. Greener districts tend also to be quieter, cleaner and less crowded, and no adjustment captures every one of those advantages. There is a further and more awkward possibility, which is that people who are already inclined to walk, to garden and to spend time outdoors may be more likely to choose a green neighbourhood in the first place, so that part of the correlation reflects who moves there rather than what living there does to them.

This is why a handful of studies with stronger designs carry weight out of proportion to their number. Several research teams have followed the same individuals through a change of address, comparing their reported wellbeing before and after a move to a greener area, and have found an improvement that is still present some years later, together with a corresponding decline among those moving the other way. A second approach has been to treat the greening of derelict land as an experiment: vacant plots in a city are cleared, planted and fenced, while similar plots nearby are left untouched, and the surrounding streets are then compared. Neither method is a clinical trial, but both remove the most obvious objection to the population studies, since the people are the same people, and both point in the same direction as the weaker evidence.

How a patch of grass and trees produces such effects is a separate question, and the candidate explanations are neither mutually exclusive nor equally well supported. The first is physical activity: green space is held to encourage walking and play. The evidence here is more mixed than one might expect, since much of the activity recorded is done by people who would have exercised somewhere in any case. The second is straightforwardly physical. Vegetation intercepts particles, muffles traffic noise, and shades and cools the ground beneath it, and in a heatwave the difference of a few degrees between a shaded street and a bare one is a matter of survival for the old and the ill; of all the mechanisms proposed, this is the best established. A third is social: a shared and pleasant outdoor space brings neighbours into casual contact, and casual contact is the raw material of the loose acquaintance that protects people against isolation. The fourth is psychological. Concentrated attention of the kind that city streets and screens demand is tiring, whereas a natural scene holds the attention without effort and so allows the tired faculty to recover; the experimental support for this is modest in size but has proved durable. The practical lesson is that these benefits can be separated. A strip of planting along a motorway that nobody can enter delivers the cooling and the filtering and nothing else.

It follows that the measure by which provision is almost always reported — the total area of green space per thousand residents — is close to useless. Area says nothing about whether the space is reachable, usable or used. Distance is the first and harshest filter: the proportion of residents who visit a park regularly falls away sharply once it is further than a few minutes' walk from the door, so that a dozen small squares will be used where one great lawn on the edge of the district will not. After distance come the things that determine whether a visit is repeated: whether the place is well maintained rather than neglected, whether it feels safe, particularly to women and to the elderly, and whether it offers shade, seating and drinking water. Variety of planting appears to matter as well; the available work suggests that a mixture of trees, shrubs and rough grass does more for wellbeing, as it does for wildlife, than the same area of mown turf. None of these qualities appears in a hectare count, and a city that manages its parks by that number will build the wrong ones.

There is also the question of who gets them. Green space is distributed across almost every city in the same pattern: least of it in the poorest and most densely built districts, which are also the hottest, the noisiest and the most exposed to traffic fumes, and whose residents have the least opportunity to leave the city at weekends. Those with most to gain have least to use. The obvious remedy, which is to plant where provision is worst, runs into a difficulty that was not anticipated when the first such programmes began. A neighbourhood made more attractive becomes more expensive; rents and prices rise around a new park, and some of the households the improvement was intended to serve are in time displaced by households who can pay more, a process that has been given the sardonic name of green gentrification. The answer to this is certainly not to withhold trees from poor streets. It is that a greening programme not accompanied by protection for the tenants living there will, in the end, deliver its benefits to somebody else.

What, then, is an honest summary? Access to green space appears to produce a small improvement in the health and the contentment of a great many people, at a cost that is low and an effect that lasts for as long as the space is maintained. That profile — modest benefit, very wide reach, durable, cheap — is precisely the profile of the public health measures that have historically done the most good, and it is also, unfortunately, the profile that is easiest to oversell. When a park is presented as a substitute for mental health provision, or when street trees are offered as a serious answer to a city's carbon emissions, the claim goes well beyond anything the research will bear, and each such claim makes the defensible ones easier to dismiss. The useful conclusion is an unglamorous one. A park is not an ornament added when the building is finished, nor a cure for the failures of everything else. It is infrastructure, and like the drains and the lighting it should be planned where people actually live, budgeted for, and maintained in the years after the ribbon has been cut.

Sleep is awkward to define and easy to recognise. Rather than argue about what is happening inside the head, researchers use a short list of behavioural signs. A sleeping animal takes up a posture, and usually a place, that is typical of its species. It becomes much less responsive to the world around it, so that a sound or a movement which would ordinarily produce a reaction produces none. The state can be ended by a strong enough disturbance, which is what separates sleep from a coma or from anaesthesia. And if the animal is kept awake, it afterwards sleeps longer or more deeply than usual, an effect known as rebound. Measured against this list, sleep has been found not only in mammals and birds but in fish, in insects such as the fruit fly, and even in the jellyfish, which has no brain at all.

In mammals and birds, electrical recording divides sleep into two conditions so different that it is slightly misleading to give them a single name. In slow-wave sleep the cells of the cortex fire together in long, synchronised bursts, so that the brain produces large, slow waves; breathing and heart rate are steady and the body can move. In the second state, called rapid eye movement or REM sleep after the darting of the eyes beneath the closed lids, the pattern of brain activity is almost indistinguishable from waking, while the muscles of the body lose their tone so completely that the animal is briefly paralysed. It is from REM sleep that a disturbed sleeper wakes with the clearest sense of having dreamed.

The arrangement raises an obvious problem for an animal that must keep working while it sleeps. A dolphin is an air-breathing mammal in water, and it cannot afford to stop swimming or to stop rising to the surface. Dolphins meet this difficulty by sleeping with one half of the brain at a time: slow waves appear in one hemisphere while the other stays awake, and the eye on the opposite side of the body is closed while its partner remains open. After a period the two halves change over. Several birds can do the same. Where a row of ducks rests together on the ground, the birds at either end of the row tend to sleep with their outer eye open and the matching half of the brain awake, while those in the middle, screened by their neighbours, close both eyes.

A few birds appear to sleep while flying. Recorders small enough to be carried by a large seabird have captured the slow waves of sleep in frigatebirds during long crossings of open ocean, mostly in one hemisphere at a time and mostly while the bird was circling upwards on a rising current of warm air rather than flapping. The totals were small, a matter of minutes a day against many hours on land, which suggests that a bird in the air sleeps as little as it can manage. Swifts are thought to do something similar, since individuals of some species stay airborne for months on end between breeding seasons and cannot be sleeping on a branch.

Animals that are hunted face a different difficulty: a body that takes a long time to get up is a body that is easily caught. A horse can doze on its feet because an arrangement of tendons and ligaments in its legs locks the joints and holds its weight with almost no effort from the muscles. That trick will not serve for REM sleep, in which muscle tone is lost, so a horse must lie down for a short period each day if it is to have any REM sleep at all. Horses kept in a place where they never feel safe enough to lie down eventually begin to collapse from the lack of it.

How much sleep an animal needs varies enormously. A brown bat may spend the greater part of the twenty-four hours asleep. An elephant, recorded in the wild with a device fitted to its trunk, sleeps only about two hours a day, and will go without sleep altogether for a night or more while travelling. The sloth was long presented as the champion sleeper on the strength of measurements made in zoos; when sloths were fitted with recorders and followed in the forest, they proved to sleep several hours less than their captive relatives, a result that has made researchers cautious about every figure gathered in captivity. Across species the broad pattern is that small animals with fast metabolisms sleep more than large ones, and that predators sleep more than the animals they prey on, although the exceptions are numerous.

Why any of it happens is still argued over, and the arguments are not exclusive. The oldest proposal is that sleep saves energy, by shutting an animal down during the hours when it could not feed or hunt efficiently in any case. A second is that sleep is a form of safety, keeping an animal still and hidden when being active would expose it. A third concerns maintenance: fluid moves more freely through the narrow spaces of the brain during slow-wave sleep than during waking, which may help to carry away the waste products of the day. A fourth concerns learning. When an animal has spent a day finding its way through a maze, the patterns of activity recorded while it learned the route are replayed during the sleep that follows, and the connections involved are reinforced, so that memories formed during the day survive better than they otherwise would.

Whatever the purpose, it is plainly not optional. Rats prevented from sleeping for long enough lose control of their body temperature, eat more and more while losing weight, and die within a few weeks. Hibernation, incidentally, is not a long sleep and should not be confused with one: the body is cold, the brain is largely inactive, and animals rousing from it sleep heavily for days, exactly as though the weeks of cold had left them short of sleep.

A great medieval cathedral was the largest and most expensive object its region would ever produce, and almost nobody who began one lived to see it finished. Work went forward in campaigns rather than at a steady pace: a bishop raised money, a few bays went up, the money ran out, and the site stood quiet until a new benefactor, a fresh wave of gifts or the arrival of pilgrims at a shrine made it possible to start again. Decades, and sometimes centuries, separated the first stone from the last. Because of this, the east end of the church, containing the high altar, was generally completed first and walled off, so that services could be held there while the nave beyond was still a building site. It also explains why so many cathedrals change style as the eye travels westwards.

The buildings that we call Gothic were made possible by three devices used together. The pointed arch carries its load more steeply downwards than a round one, and, more usefully still, arches of different widths can be made to rise to the same height, which allows a vault to be built over a bay that is not square. The rib vault concentrates the weight of a ceiling onto a framework of stone ribs, which deliver it to a few points rather than spreading it along the whole wall. The flying buttress then carries the outward thrust from those points across the open air to a heavy pier standing clear of the building. Once the thrust has somewhere else to go, the wall between the piers is no longer holding the roof up. It can be opened, and the result is the cathedral as a cage of stone filled with glass.

Directing all this was the master mason, a craftsman who had worked his way up with a chisel and who combined the roles later divided between architect, engineer and site manager. He worked from a lodge, a timber building against the wall of the church where the masons cut stone, kept their tools and ate. Drawings on parchment were rare, small and costly, and the serious design work was done at full size. Many lodges had a tracing floor, a wide surface of soft plaster on which the outline of a window, an arch or a moulding could be set out at its true dimensions with a compass and a straight edge, scraped away and drawn again. From these full-size outlines the masons cut thin templates in wood, and every block was worked until it matched its template. The method was geometrical rather than arithmetical: proportions were generated by construction, by squares and circles drawn from one another, at a time when written calculation was laborious and few on site could do it.

The material itself had to be found, shaped and moved. Where a good bed of stone lay near the site the builders quarried it there; otherwise it came from far off, and the first rule of transport was that stone should be roughly shaped at the quarry, so that less weight had to be carried. Wherever a river or the sea offered a route the stone went by water, since a single barge could take what would have needed dozens of carts over bad roads. At the site each block was finished by hand, and a mason would cut a small mark of his own into the stones he had dressed so that his output could be counted and paid for; these marks can still be read on the inner faces of many walls. Cathedrals also consumed timber on an enormous scale, and a large site kept its own smiths busy doing little but sharpening chisels.

Raising the stone was a problem of its own. An arch cannot stand until its last stone is in place, so each one was built over a wooden framework, called centring, which held the blocks in position until the mortar had set and could then be struck away and used again. Scaffolding rose with the walls, its horizontal poles resting in square holes deliberately left in the masonry, some of which were never filled in. For lifting, the great machine was a crane driven by a large wooden wheel, inside which one or two men walked as though climbing an endless staircase, turning a drum that wound the rope. The crane was mounted on the walls themselves and moved upwards as they grew. To grip the block, masons cut a tapering slot in its upper face and fitted into it an iron device known as a lewis, whose wedge-shaped pieces were pulled tight by the weight of the stone, so that the heavier the load, the firmer the hold.

The pace of the work was set, in the end, by mortar. Medieval mortar was made from lime, and lime mortar hardens slowly, drawing in air over months rather than curing in hours. A wall that rose too quickly could squeeze and spread the soft joints beneath it, and frost reaching mortar that had not yet set would destroy it altogether. Masons therefore worked through the warmer months only, and at the end of the season the tops of unfinished walls were capped with straw, dung or turf to keep the frost out until spring. The need to let one stage settle before loading it with the next is one reason why a cathedral could not have been built quickly even if the money had never run short.

Not everything stood. The builders were working beyond any tested experience, and the limit was found at Beauvais in northern France, where the choir was raised higher than any before it and part of its vault came down a few years after completion. It was rebuilt with the supports doubled, and the church was never finished as planned. Elsewhere the warnings were quieter: cracks appeared, piers leaned, and later masons added flying buttresses to buildings that had been designed without them. What the sites did not use was the army of pious volunteers of popular imagination. Processions of townspeople dragging carts of stone did occur, and were remembered because they were unusual; the walls were built by paid men, by quarriers, masons, carpenters, smiths, glaziers and plumbers who moved from one great project to the next, and the chief difficulty for any bishop was less a shortage of faith than a shortage of cash.

title.t: Who Decides What the Machines Will Do?

runs.t: Arguments about machines and work follow a script so familiar that both parts can be recited in advance. One side announces that a new technology is about to make human labour unnecessary. The other replies, patiently, that this has been said at every stage of industrial history and has never come true: mechanisation destroyed particular occupations, but it also made goods cheaper, created demand that had not existed, and brought into being whole categories of work that nobody had been able to imagine. The quantity of work in a society is not a fixed lump to be divided up, and anyone who assumes that it is will reach gloomy conclusions by arithmetic alone. All of this is correct, and it is also beside the point, because it is an answer to a question that very few people are actually asking. The serious worry has never been that a day will arrive on which there is no work left to do. It is a worry about who loses, at what moment in their life, and on what terms.

The machine-breakers of the early industrial period have become a byword for futile resistance to progress, which is unfair to them and unhelpful to us. They were not ignorant of machinery; many were highly skilled men whose trade had taken years to learn and could be acquired in weeks once a machine did the difficult part. Within their own working lives the value of that skill collapsed, and the wages that had supported a household fell to a level that would not. It is true that their grandchildren found employment in industries which could not have existed without the machines their grandfathers attacked. But a recovery that takes two generations is not a recovery for the generation that pays for it, and a benefit distributed across a whole society is no answer to a cost concentrated on a few thousand households in a single valley. Averages conceal precisely the thing that is at issue.

Is the present wave genuinely unlike the earlier ones? Something can be said for the claim. Previous machines took over physical operations and, later, arithmetic; the systems now spreading operate on language, images and judgement, which widens the range of tasks exposed and means that the people affected include many who assumed their work was protected by education. Yet confidence about the pace of the change is not warranted by the record. Tasks that were declared to be months away have remained stubbornly undone for a decade, while others that were thought to be safely human gave way almost without warning. The honest position is that the direction of travel is reasonably clear and the speed of it is not, and arrangements built on a particular date are likely to fail. What follows is not paralysis but a preference for measures that work whether the change arrives in five years or in fifty.

The most important question is the one that is least often framed as a question at all, which is where the gains go. When a process is automated, the value that used to be paid out in wages does not vanish; it is redistributed. It may go to the owners of the equipment as profit, to customers in the form of lower prices, or to the workers who remain, whose output per hour has risen. Which of these happens is not determined by the machine. It depends on how concentrated the industry is, on the bargaining strength of employees, on how the proceeds are taxed, on who owns the equipment, and on whether people displaced from one occupation can get the training that would let them enter another. Technology fixes what is possible; institutions decide the shares. A complaint about automation is therefore almost always a complaint about an arrangement, and arrangements, unlike physics, are open to amendment.

If the loss were only a loss of income, the remedy would be straightforward, and the various proposals for paying people an income whether or not they are employed would settle the matter. The evidence from the study of unemployment suggests that it would not. People who lose work report the disappearance of things that money does not restore: a shape to the day, a reason to leave the house, contact with people who are not family, a position that can be named when strangers ask, and the sense of being depended upon by somebody. Their health and their contentment decline further than the fall in their income can explain, and those who find new work of a similar kind recover in a way that those who merely receive money do not. A payment addresses the part of the loss that is easiest to measure and the smallest part of what is actually gone.

None of which should be turned into a defence of work as such, and here the argument often goes astray. A great deal of employment is monotonous, physically damaging or humiliating, and it is noticeable that the warmest tributes to the dignity of labour are composed by people whose own working days are varied, autonomous and comfortable. A machine that takes over the lifting in a warehouse, the inspection of a sewer or the handling of dangerous chemicals removes a genuine harm from somebody's life, and it is not progress to keep such jobs in existence on the grounds that they are jobs. The reasonable aim is fewer bad jobs rather than more of them, which means that the objection cannot be to automation in general. It must be to the particular way in which the costs and the benefits are currently allocated.

Put the strands together and the ethical question comes into focus. It is not whether machines should do work that people now do; much of that transfer is desirable and all of it is coming. It is who decides which tasks are handed over, at what speed, which people are expected to absorb the disruption, and who collects what is saved. Those decisions are made by companies choosing what to invest in, by governments choosing what to tax, subsidise and teach, and occasionally by organised employees choosing what to accept. They are choices, and they could be made differently. The one response that is certainly wrong is to speak of automation as though it were the weather: something that happens to a society, about which the only sensible attitude is to carry an umbrella.

How a colony of insects tells its members where to find the next meal.

A honeybee colony may contain tens of thousands of workers, and in the course of a summer day it has to find and exploit patches of flowers that are scattered over many square kilometres of countryside and that may come into bloom and fade within a week. No individual bee can survey such an area, and there is nobody in the hive to issue orders. What the colony has instead is a system of communication in which a forager that has found something worth collecting is able to tell her nestmates where it is. The system was worked out in the first half of the twentieth century by the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch, whose patient experiments with marked bees and dishes of sugar water eventually earned him a share of a Nobel Prize.

A forager that has returned from a rewarding patch does not settle down quietly. She climbs on to the vertical face of a comb, pushes into the crowd of workers there and begins to dance. If the flowers are close to the hive, the dance is a simple one: the bee runs in a tight circle, reverses, circles again, and goes on reversing for several seconds or more. This round dance says nothing about direction. It announces only that something worth having lies somewhere in the immediate neighbourhood, and the bees that follow it leave the hive and search in all directions around it. They are not, however, searching blindly, because the scent of the flowers she has visited still clings to her body, and a sample of the nectar itself is passed from her mouth to theirs.

When the food is further off, the forager performs a quite different movement, the waggle dance. She runs forward in a straight line, shaking her abdomen rapidly from side to side and producing a buzzing vibration as she goes, then loops back to her starting point, to one side on one circuit and to the other side on the next, so that her path traces a flattened figure of eight. The straight portion, known as the waggle run, carries the message, and two of its features matter. The first is its angle. The comb hangs vertically in the dark, so the bee uses gravity in place of the sky: a run made straight up the comb means that the food lies in the direction of the sun, while a run thirty degrees to the left of vertical means that the food lies thirty degrees to the left of the sun. The second feature is duration. The longer the waggle run lasts, the further the forager has flown, so that distance is expressed as time rather than as length. A single dance may repeat the run dozens of times, and since it is performed in the darkness of the hive the bees that follow cannot see it at all; they press close behind the dancer, touch her with their antennae and pick up the vibrations she sends through the comb.

A direction given relative to the sun has an obvious weakness, which is that the sun moves. Foragers solve this by keeping track of the passage of time, and a dancer who is detained inside the hive will slowly alter the angle of her run, as though following a sun she cannot see. Cloud is a smaller problem than it appears. A patch of blue sky is enough, because a bee can detect the pattern of polarised light that the sky produces, and that pattern reveals where the sun must be.

The dance reports more than a position. The richer the source — the sweeter the nectar, the easier the flowers are to work, the shorter the flight — the more vigorous and the more persistent the dance, while a mediocre find produces a brief dance or none at all. Since the number of recruits that leave depends on how long and how energetically the dancer performs, the number of foragers visiting a site rises quickly while it remains productive and falls away when it does not. No bee compares the patches available to the colony, and none needs to.

For many years this account was not universally accepted. A number of researchers argued that recruits in fact found the food by smell, following the odour of the flowers and of the foraging bees themselves, and that the dance, however elegant, told them nothing they could use. The objection was a fair one, since in ordinary circumstances the two explanations predict much the same behaviour. Two kinds of experiment eventually settled the question. In the first, a mechanical model of a bee was made to perform waggle runs inside a hive, and recruits flew out to the place the model had indicated, although no bee had ever been there. In the second, individual recruits were fitted with tiny transponders and tracked by radar as they left the hive; they flew the course that the dance had specified, and then began to search when they reached the end of it.

Other signals are exchanged on the same crowded dance floor. A forager who comes back loaded with nectar and cannot quickly find a house bee to take it from her will perform a tremble dance, walking slowly about with her legs shaking, and the effect of this is to recruit more workers to the business of receiving and storing nectar rather than to the flowers. There is also a short vibrating pulse, delivered by one bee butting its head against a dancer, which makes the dancer break off; it is given by bees that have met with danger at the site being advertised, and it damps down recruitment to a dangerous place. The same waggle dance is used for a quite different purpose when a colony divides and swarms. Scouts go out to look for a cavity in which the swarm can live, and each returns to dance on the surface of the clustered bees for the site she has found, the persistence of her dance reflecting how good she judges it to be. Scouts are drawn away to inspect the sites that rivals are advertising, and dancing for the poorer cavities gradually ceases, until almost every dancer is advertising the same address and the swarm flies to it.

title.t: A Promise on a Piece of Paper

runs.t: For most of history, money was a thing of value in itself: a silver coin was worth what the silver in it was worth. Such money has one great disadvantage: it is heavy. A merchant who wished to buy goods at the other end of a kingdom had either to carry a chest of coin along roads where robbery was a serious risk, or to find some way of making a payment without moving metal at all. Paper money began as an answer to that practical difficulty, and only later became a currency in its own right. The crucial step was a change in what the object in the hand actually was. A coin is wealth; a note is a claim on wealth, a promise made by somebody else, and the whole history of paper money is the history of how far such promises can be trusted.

The first such promises on paper that we know of were issued in Tang dynasty China, more than a thousand years ago. Traders bringing goods to the capital were reluctant to carry the proceeds home in copper coin, and arrangements grew up under which the coin was deposited with an agent in one city and a certificate issued which could be presented for coin in another. The documents were nicknamed flying cash, and they were not money in the full sense: they were not intended to circulate, and each one was a record of a particular deposit made by a particular person. What they did show was that a piece of paper could do the work of a cart-load of metal.

Notes that genuinely passed from hand to hand appeared a little later, in the province of Sichuan, and the reason they appeared there is instructive. Copper was scarce in the region and the local coinage was made of iron, which is worth far less by weight. The result was a currency so bulky that a household buying a roll of cloth might have to move a load of metal heavier than the cloth itself. Merchant houses in the provincial capital began to accept deposits of coin and to issue printed receipts for them, and because everyone knew the houses that issued them these receipts were soon being handed on in payment rather than taken back for metal. In the early eleventh century the authorities, troubled by the failure of some of these private issuers, suppressed them and took the business over, printing notes themselves which were valid within a defined region and for a fixed period and which were supported by a reserve of coin. This is generally regarded as the first paper currency issued by a government anywhere.

Under the Mongol emperors of the Yuan dynasty, paper money reached its medieval height. Notes printed on paper made from mulberry bark were issued across an empire that stretched far beyond China proper, and they were declared the only lawful means of payment: a merchant who refused to accept them was liable to severe punishment, and gold and silver were to be handed in to the treasury in exchange for paper. Travellers from Europe, where every payment still meant counting out metal, found the arrangement astonishing, and the Venetian Marco Polo devoted an admiring chapter of his account of his travels to the emperor who, as he saw it, turned bark into treasure.

The weakness of the system was not technical but political. A government that can print its own money is a government that can meet a deficit without raising taxes, and successive Chinese dynasties did exactly that. Each new issue reduced the value of the notes already in circulation; prices rose, confidence fell, and people who could do so hoarded metal. By the fifteenth century the notes of the Ming dynasty had lost almost all their purchasing power, and the state eventually gave up the attempt. For several centuries afterwards China conducted its large transactions in silver, weighed out and assessed for purity at each payment — a cumbersome method, but one that no official could inflate with a printing block. The episode established the lesson that every later issuer has had to learn: paper money costs almost nothing to make, and that is precisely its danger.

Europe arrived at the same institution by a different route. Merchants there had long used bills of exchange, written instructions by which a debt incurred in one city could be settled by a correspondent in another, and these too allowed trade to be financed without shipping coin. The decisive development came in seventeenth-century London, where goldsmiths, who possessed strong rooms, took in coin for safe keeping and gave depositors written receipts promising to return it on demand. Such receipts began to circulate, and the goldsmiths noticed that only a small proportion of the coin they held was ever called for at any one time, so that they could safely lend out more in receipts than they actually held in metal. Sweden, where the main coinage consisted of copper plates of extraordinary weight, was the first European country to issue true banknotes, in the seventeenth century; the bank that issued them printed more than it could redeem and failed within a few years. The Bank of England, founded in 1694 in order to lend money to a government at war, issued notes that promised to pay the bearer on demand, and that formula survives, long after the promise itself has changed its meaning.

Over the following two centuries the right to issue notes was gradually concentrated in a single institution in each country, and the promise they carried was tied to a fixed quantity of gold. That tie proved to be a fair-weather arrangement. Convertibility was suspended in wartime, restored with difficulty, suspended again, and finally abandoned altogether in the early 1970s. What a modern note promises is therefore nothing more definite than itself. Its value rests on the restraint of the institution that issues it and on the fact that the state will accept it in payment of taxes and the courts will recognise it in settlement of debts. Cash is now in retreat, as payments move to entries transferred between accounts, but the principle being transferred is the one that was invented, lost and invented again over a thousand years.

runs.t: In every country that receives migrants, and in a great many that do not, children arrive at school speaking a language other than the one the school teaches in. What a school should do about this is among the most bitterly contested questions in education. Two intuitions pull in opposite directions. The first is that a child who needs to learn a language should hear and use as much of it as possible, and that time spent on anything else is time wasted. The second is that a child learns most readily through a language already understood, and that a school which ignores what a child brings is throwing away the only foundation available. Much of the heat in the argument comes from the fact that the phrase bilingual education is applied to arrangements whose aims have almost nothing in common.

It is worth separating them. In a transitional programme, the home language is used as a temporary bridge: children are taught the curriculum partly in it while they acquire the language of the school, and are moved into ordinary classes after two or three years, once they are judged able to cope with the language of instruction. The aim is competence in the majority language, and the home language is a means to that end. A maintenance programme, by contrast, goes on using the home language throughout, on the grounds that literacy in it is worth having for its own sake. A dual-language programme is different again: two groups of children, speakers of each of the two languages, are taught together, each group learning the other's language, with the intention that all of them leave school able to use both. Finally there is structured immersion, in which everything is taught in the majority language, but in a simplified and carefully supported form, the home language being used only occasionally, to explain something a child has not understood. The label on a programme therefore tells an observer very little about what happens inside it.

The case for teaching through the home language rests on a straightforward observation about transfer. A child who has learned to read in one language does not have to learn to read all over again in another. The understanding of what print is for, and the habit of predicting what a sentence will say, are not tied to a particular vocabulary. Subject knowledge behaves in the same way. Fractions learned in one language do not have to be learned again in another; only the words for them do. There is a further point about how long it takes to be ready to learn in a new language. Children pick up conversational fluency quickly, often within a year or two, and a child who chats easily in the playground is widely assumed to be ready for the rest of the timetable. The language of textbooks and examinations, however — abstract, dense, full of constructions nobody uses in speech — takes a good deal longer to master, and a pupil who is treated as fluent before reaching that point may sit through years of lessons understanding only a fraction of them.

The case against is equally serious. The simplest version of it concerns time: hours spent learning in the home language are hours not spent in the language the child will be examined in and will work in, and in a crowded timetable something has to give. Critics also point to the risk that children remain in separate classes long after they could manage in the mainstream, in a track which, being separate, attracts lower expectations. Then there are the practical obstacles. A single city school may contain children speaking dozens of languages, and no school can staff a programme for each. Even where one language dominates, teachers who are fluent and literate in it, trained in the curriculum and qualified to teach are often simply not available, and suitable books and materials may not exist. It is also a mistake to assume that migrant parents all want the home language in school. Many, anxious that their children should get on, ask for immersion and regard anything else as a distraction.

What does the research show? Less than either side claims, and for reasons that are built into the problem. Children are not allocated to programmes at random: families choose, and schools select, so that the pupils in one kind of programme may differ from those in another before any teaching has taken place. Programmes bearing the same name vary enormously in how they are staffed and run, and outcomes are measured at different ages and by different instruments. Reviews that pool the available studies tend to report a modest advantage for programmes that make substantial use of the home language, an advantage that is clearer on long-term measures than on tests taken soon after a programme begins. But the advantage is smaller than its advocates suggest, and the difference between a well-run and a badly run version of the same model is usually larger than the difference between one model and another.

One body of evidence deserves particular care, because it is so often misused. The French immersion programmes developed in Canada, in which English-speaking children are taught largely in French, have been studied for decades and are by any measure a success: the pupils become competent in French without falling behind in English or in other subjects. This is regularly cited as proof that immersion works and that teaching through the home language is unnecessary. The inference is unsound. Those children were learning an additional language while their first language remained the dominant and prestigious one in the society around them, supported by their families, the media and the law, and participation was voluntary. Adding a second language to a secure first language is a quite different undertaking from replacing a home language with the language of a majority that often regards the first as a handicap, and results from the one case cannot simply be carried across to the other.

It is worth noticing how such questions are actually decided. In one American state, voters passed a measure in the late 1990s that largely prohibited teaching in languages other than English in public schools, and nearly twenty years later voters in the same state reversed much of that restriction. The evidence available on the two occasions was not greatly different; the mood of the electorate was. Debates about language in school are rarely only about attainment: they are also about national belonging and about who is expected to adapt to whom, and such questions are not settled by test scores.

The useful question is therefore not which model wins, but under what conditions a given approach works: for how long the home language should carry part of the teaching, what training the teachers need, and how to judge the point at which a child is genuinely ready to learn in the new language. Almost everyone now agrees that a child's home language is an asset rather than an obstacle. What remains in dispute is how much of a school's limited time and money should be spent protecting it — a question about priorities, which no experiment can answer on its own.

Why the same eruption can cool the world for a year and warm it for a hundred thousand.

A large volcanic eruption is one of the very few natural events capable of altering the temperature of the whole planet within a few months, and it is also one of the most frequently misunderstood. In the weeks after a spectacular eruption the question usually asked is whether the volcano will warm the world or cool it, as though the answer had to be one or the other. An eruption does both, but on two timescales so far apart that they almost never compete. Over a year or two a big eruption cools the surface, by placing material high in the atmosphere where it intercepts sunlight before it can arrive. Over hundreds of thousands of years volcanism warms the surface, by adding to the air a gas that the planet has no rapid means of removing. Confusing the two is the commonest error in popular accounts of the subject.

What leaves a volcano is a mixture of solid fragments and gas. The solids range from blocks the size of a car to the fine shattered glass that is loosely called ash. Almost all of this material is heavy enough to fall back to the ground within hours or days, and even the finest ash is normally out of the air within a few weeks; it can ruin a harvest or bury a town, but it has little to do with global temperature. The gases are a different matter. Most of what a volcano exhales is water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide, with much smaller quantities of sulphur dioxide and other compounds. It is the sulphur dioxide, a minor component by weight, that does nearly all the work. Once in the atmosphere it reacts with water to form enormous numbers of microscopic droplets of sulphuric acid. Each droplet is far too small to see, but collectively they form a thin haze that scatters a fraction of the incoming sunlight back towards space, so that slightly less of it reaches the ground.

Whether that haze matters depends almost entirely on how high the eruption column rises. The lower atmosphere, in which our weather takes place, is constantly stirred and constantly wet, and anything suspended in it is washed out by rainfall within a matter of weeks. Above it lies the stratosphere, a calm, dry, layered region in which there is no rain to clean the air. An eruption violent enough to drive its plume through the boundary between the two delivers its sulphur into a place where the droplets can remain for a year or more, drifting slowly away from the latitude at which they were injected. Latitude therefore matters as well. Because the high-altitude circulation carries material away from the equator towards both poles, an eruption in the tropics can spread its haze over both hemispheres, while one at high latitudes tends to affect mainly the hemisphere in which it occurred. A modest eruption in Iceland and a modest eruption in Indonesia are not equivalent events.

The clearest demonstrations come from the historical record. The eruption of Tambora in Indonesia in 1815 was followed by a summer so cold and wet in Europe and eastern North America that crops failed, grain prices rose steeply and 1816 became known as the year without a summer. Much later, and far better measured, the eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines in 1991 lowered the average temperature of the global surface by roughly half a degree Celsius over the following year, before the haze thinned and temperatures recovered. Half a degree sounds trivial. It is in fact comparable in size to a good deal of the warming accumulated over the twentieth century, which is a useful reminder of how little it takes to change a planetary average, and of how short-lived such a change can be when the cause is removed.

Eruptions that no one recorded in writing can still be dated, because the atmosphere files its own accounts. Snow falling on Greenland and Antarctica is buried, compressed and preserved, and a core drilled through the resulting ice contains a layer for every year. Sulphuric acid from a stratospheric haze is deposited with the snow, so a large eruption leaves a distinct chemical signal in both polar ice sheets if it occurred in the tropics, and in only one if it did not. A second archive grows in forests. A tree adds a ring each season, and a cold, short growing season produces a ring that is unusually narrow, or one damaged by frost before the wood has hardened. When a chemical layer in the ice and a run of poor rings in the trees point to the same year, the case for a major eruption is strong, and historians can go back to the written sources to look for the famines that often followed.

The long story is the opposite of the short one. Carbon dioxide is a very weak contributor to the immediate effect of an eruption, because the quantity released even by a great explosion is small set against the amount already in the air. But carbon dioxide is not rained out. It accumulates, and over geological time the slow, unspectacular release of the gas from volcanic systems is one of the principal reasons that the planet has stayed habitable rather than freezing permanently. Episodes in the deep past in which enormous volumes of lava reached the surface over tens of thousands of years are associated with intervals of pronounced warmth, and with some of the severest crises in the history of life. It is worth stating plainly, however, that the modern figure for volcanic emissions is dwarfed by the output of industry and transport: human activity now releases far more carbon dioxide in a year than the world's volcanoes do, and the comparison is not close.

The cooling effect has nevertheless attracted interest as a model for deliberate intervention. If a haze of sulphate droplets in the stratosphere can lower the temperature of the planet by half a degree, the argument runs, then a haze maintained artificially could offset part of the warming produced by greenhouse gases, and at a cost that is small beside the cost of reducing emissions. The objections are substantial. A haze that is not renewed disappears within a few years, so any such scheme would have to be continued indefinitely, and abandoning it suddenly would release the suppressed warming all at once. Reflecting sunlight does nothing about the carbon dioxide itself, which would continue to acidify the oceans. The effects on rainfall would not be distributed evenly, and a measure that cooled one region might dry another, with no mechanism in existence for deciding who should be compensated. Volcanoes demonstrate that the mechanism works. They say nothing about whether it could be governed.
