runs.t: A coastline is not a line but a problem. Approached from the sea at night, a low shore is invisible, a headland looks like an island, and the reef that will open a ship's hull lies a mile from anything that can be seen at all. A light placed on the shore solves two difficulties at once. It warns that a danger is near, and, if the mariner knows which light he is looking at, it also tells him where he is, which is the harder and more valuable service of the two. For most of recorded history there was no reliable way of fixing a position out of sight of land, so the sight of a known light after a long passage was the moment at which guesswork ended. Societies that depended on sea trade therefore found ways of paying for lights, usually by charging a due on every cargo landed, long before they would pay for roads of comparable usefulness.

The earliest towers were simply high places on which a fire could be kept burning. The most celebrated of them, the Pharos of Alexandria, was raised in the third century BC, was counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world, and stood for well over a thousand years before earthquakes brought it down. The Romans built lesser towers at the mouths of their harbours, including one that still survives within the walls of Dover Castle in England. In medieval Europe the work often fell to religious houses, and a chapel on a cliff with a lamp in its window might be maintained by monks who were also paid to pray for sailors. The fuel was wood and, later and more usually, coal, burned in an open iron basket at the top of the tower. Such a fire was genuinely bright, but it consumed an enormous weight of fuel, every ton of which had to be carried up by hand, and it burned worst in precisely the conditions in which it was most needed, since rain drowned it and a gale either blew it out or smothered it in its own smoke.

The hardest lights to establish were those on rocks that the sea covered at high water, and the long argument over one of them, the Eddystone reef off Plymouth, became the school in which the problem was solved. The first tower there, an elaborate wooden structure finished in 1698, was swept away in a great storm five years later, taking its builder with it. The second, completed in 1709 and built largely of wood on a stone base, lasted almost fifty years before it burned down. The third was the decisive one. Finished in 1759, it was built of stone throughout, and its designer solved the problem of a structure that the waves would try to lift rather than merely push: each block was dovetailed into its neighbours and into the course below, so that the tower behaved as a single mass, and it was bedded in a lime that would set under water instead of a mortar that would wash away. Its profile, broad at the base and curving inwards as it rose, was deliberately modelled on the trunk of an oak, a shape chosen because a tree survives the wind that fells a wall. Every wave-swept tower built since has followed the same principles.

Solving the building left the light itself, which until the end of the eighteenth century was poor. The improvement came from two directions. The first was a new oil lamp with a hollow circular wick and a glass chimney, which drew air through the middle of the flame as well as around it and so burned far more steadily and brightly than a wick in a dish. The second was optical. A flame radiates in every direction, and a light at sea needs almost all of that radiation sent outwards in a narrow horizontal band. Curved metal reflectors placed behind the lamp achieved part of this, but they absorbed a good deal of the light they handled. The answer, introduced in the 1820s, was a lens assembled from concentric rings of glass, each ring ground to the angle required to bend the light passing through it into the beam. Because the thickness of a conventional lens had been replaced by a series of thin steps, the new apparatus was lighter, cheaper and far less absorbent than a solid lens of the same power would have been, and it increased the range of a light out of all recognition. The lamps beneath it changed repeatedly over the following century, from vegetable and mineral oils to vaporised paraffin, gas and finally electricity, but the lens did not need to change at all.

A powerful light raised a new difficulty: on a coast with many lights, a brilliant one is useless if the mariner cannot tell which it is. Each station was therefore given its own pattern of flashes and intervals of darkness, and these patterns were printed in the lists of lights that every navigator carried, so that a sailor could identify a station by counting with his watch. Producing the pattern meant turning the whole lens assembly around the lamp at a precise speed. Early arrangements ran on rollers and wore out quickly; the elegant solution was to float the entire rotating structure, which might weigh several tonnes, in a shallow bath of mercury, where it could be set moving with the pressure of one hand. The motive power was clockwork, wound up by the keeper at intervals through the night, with a weight descending slowly down the centre of the tower exactly as in a longcase clock.

All of this required keepers, usually three at an isolated station so that two were always available and no man was ever alone with a body if one of them died. Their work was unromantic. They trimmed wicks, polished glass, wound the clockwork, kept a written log and painted whatever was within reach, and in bad weather they waited, sometimes for weeks beyond the date on which a relief was due. Automation ended the profession in the course of the twentieth century. Once lamps could be changed by a mechanism, failures reported by radio and the whole installation supervised from an office on shore, there was no case for keeping men on a rock, and the last keepers were withdrawn from most national services before the century ended. Satellite navigation has since removed the second of the lighthouse's two functions altogether, and a modern ship knows its position to within a few metres without looking out of the window. Lights are nevertheless still maintained, because electronics fail and the rocks do not move, and the towers themselves have acquired a new value as monuments to a period when the only way to make a coast safe was to put a man on it with a lamp.

runs.t: Few words have been absorbed into everyday speech as quickly, or as carelessly, as multitasking. It was borrowed from computing, where it describes a processor that gives short turns to several programs in succession, and it was then applied to people as though it described something they could get better at by trying. Job advertisements request it. Students claim it as a skill. The claim is usually made with some pride, and it is almost always a description of a habit rather than an ability. The borrowed word is in fact an unusually accurate one, provided it is understood in its original sense: the machine is not doing two things at once either. It is taking turns, very fast, and the costs of taking turns are the subject of this article.

The architecture of attention makes genuine simultaneity impossible for a narrow but important class of tasks. A great deal of what a person does in a day is automatic, in the technical sense that it has been practised until it no longer requires any decision: walking, chewing, following a familiar road. Automatic activities make almost no demand on the central machinery that selects and controls behaviour, and they can therefore be combined with a demanding task without harm, which is why a conversation and a well-known drive can run alongside each other quite comfortably. What cannot be combined are two tasks that both require that central machinery, because it deals with one thing at a time. Reading a sentence and composing a different one, listening to an argument and drafting a reply, are activities that must queue. The strong impression of doing both at once is produced by switching rapidly between them, and the impression is convincing because the switching is not itself something we can observe.

Switching is not free. Laboratory work on the point is straightforward and remarkably consistent: when people alternate between two tasks, each of which they can perform quickly on its own, they are slower and make more errors than when they complete one and then the other. Part of the loss is mechanical reconfiguration, the mental equivalent of changing tools. A larger part appears to be residue. Attention does not detach cleanly, and for some seconds after a switch a portion of it remains occupied with the task just abandoned, degrading the task now in hand. This is why an interruption costs more than the time it takes. The real expense is not the two minutes spent answering the question but the effort of rebuilding afterwards the state the interrupted work required: the half-formed plan, the three figures held in mind, the sense of where the argument was going. Work that has to be reassembled from the beginning several times in an afternoon may never reach the depth it needed.

One might expect that people who do this constantly would at least have grown efficient at it. The evidence points the other way, and it is among the more robust findings in the field. When volunteers are sorted by how much media multitasking they report in daily life, those at the heavy end perform worse, not better, on tasks that require irrelevant information to be ignored, worse on tasks requiring an item to be held in memory while something else is attended to, and, awkwardly, worse at switching between tasks. They are also markedly more confident of their performance. Whether heavy multitasking erodes the ability to filter, or whether people who filter poorly are drawn to environments that keep interrupting them, is not settled by this kind of comparison and should not be asserted. What can be said is that the self-assessment is unreliable, and that an activity which feels productive while it is being performed is weak evidence that it is.

A fair account must register the counter-arguments. Not every combination is costly, and the automatic category is larger than the sceptics sometimes allow; the objection is to specific pairings, not to doing more than one thing in an hour. Nor is a familiar drive dangerous merely because the driver is talking, for as long as the driving stays routine. The difficulty arrives at the moment it stops being routine, when the lorry ahead brakes without warning and the resources that the unexpected event requires are already committed elsewhere. There is also a persistent claim that a very small proportion of people suffer no measurable penalty at all from dividing attention. Such claims deserve interest, but they deserve caution too: a tiny minority identified by a test is exactly the sort of result that shrinks when the test is repeated, and in any case almost everyone who believes they belong to this group has been shown, by the paragraph above, to be an unreliable judge of the matter.

Where the discussion goes wrong is in treating the whole question as one of personal discipline. Modern working environments are built to interrupt. Messages arrive with a sound and a moving banner, both designed by people whose purpose was to make the message impossible to ignore. Open-plan offices put every conversation within earshot. An expectation has grown up, in many organisations, that a message should be answered within minutes, so that the worker who concentrates is the worker who appears unresponsive. It is worth adding that the figures circulated about all this should be handled sceptically: the striking numbers quoted for the hours or the billions lost to interruption every year are repeated far more confidently than their original basis justifies, and a weak statistic is a poor foundation for a sound argument. The argument does not need it. Self-interruption deserves mention as well, since studies of people at work find that a large share of switches are initiated by the worker rather than by anyone else, and a habit of reaching for a device during any dull moment is not something an employer can switch off.

The practical advice that follows is unglamorous and tolerably well supported: protect blocks of time in which notification is impossible rather than merely discouraged, gather similar small tasks and do them together, and expect the first minutes of any resumed work to be unproductive, because they will be. But advice directed at individuals cannot carry the whole weight. If attention is a limited resource, an organisation that fragments it has made a design decision, in the same way that it makes a decision about lighting or about the height of a desk, and it is odd that the first is so rarely examined while the second is regulated. The useful conclusion is not that people should try harder to do several things at once. It is that the heaviest costs of divided attention arise from the way environments are arranged, and that they can be reduced by arranging them differently.

title.t: The Unseen Journey of the Eel

runs.t: For as long as people have fished the rivers of Europe they have caught eels, and for most of that time nobody could say where an eel came from. Fishermen took them from ponds, ditches and estuaries, and found that the animals they cut open contained no eggs and no recognisable reproductive organs at all. Eels seemed to appear in waters that had no connection with any other, including isolated pools, and they could be seen on wet nights crossing damp grass from one ditch to the next. Aristotle, who examined the question as carefully as anyone in the ancient world, concluded that eels were not born but formed spontaneously out of mud. Variations on that idea survived for centuries, and the puzzle of the eel’s origin was still unsolved when biology had explained the life cycle of almost every other European fish.

The answer, when it came, was assembled from the sea rather than from the river. Early in the twentieth century the Danish scientist Johannes Schmidt began a long series of Atlantic voyages, towing fine nets at depth and collecting the small, leaf-shaped larvae that were by then known to be young eels. His method was simple in principle: wherever he sailed, he measured the larvae he caught, reasoning that the smallest ones must be the newest and so would be found nearest to the place where they had hatched. Year after year the catches led him west and south, and the tiniest specimens of all came from the Sargasso Sea, a warm, still region of the western Atlantic bounded not by coasts but by circling currents. Schmidt concluded that the European eel spawns there and nowhere else. A century later this remains the accepted account, although no adult European eel has ever been observed spawning in the wild, and the eggs themselves have never been collected from the open ocean.

The creature that hatches is so unlike an eel that it was described as a separate species before anyone realised what it was. A leptocephalus is flattened from side to side, shaped like a willow leaf and almost perfectly transparent, with a body of jelly-like tissue and a thread of gut. It is a feeble swimmer, and for the crossing of the Atlantic it is carried rather than carrying itself, riding the broad drift of warm water that runs north-east towards Europe. The journey takes a year or more, and the larva feeds on fine organic material suspended in the surface water rather than hunting prey.

Arrival at the edge of the continental shelf triggers the first of several transformations. The leaf-shaped larva shrinks, thickens and becomes a glass eel: a transparent miniature of the adult, still without pigment, so clear that the spine can be seen through the flesh. Glass eels gather in estuaries in winter and spring, and use the rising tide to carry themselves inland, holding position near the bottom while the water falls. As they take on colour they are known as elvers, and they begin to push upstream, climbing wet stone and weed around obstacles that would stop most fish.

There follows the long, obscure middle of the eel’s life. In rivers, lakes, marshes and estuaries the animal becomes a yellow eel, so called for the dull olive and brass of its flanks, and it may remain in this stage for anything from a few years to several decades, hunting at night, lying under stones by day and growing very slowly in cold water. One of the stranger features of the species belongs to this period. An eel’s sex is not fixed when the egg is fertilised; it is settled much later, and appears to depend on the conditions in which the young animal grows, with crowded waters producing a different balance of males and females from sparsely populated ones.

At last something prompts the eel to leave. Over a few months its body is rebuilt for a journey it will make only once. The eyes enlarge greatly and their pigments shift towards the blue of deep water; the pectoral fins broaden; the back darkens and the flanks turn a metallic silver that makes the animal hard to see from above or below. The gut degenerates and the eel stops feeding altogether, so that the entire crossing must be paid for out of stored fat. These silver eels drop downstream on dark, rainy autumn nights and disappear into the Atlantic, and almost nothing is known of what happens next, beyond the fact that they are thought to die after spawning.

The European eel is now in serious trouble. The number of glass eels reaching European estuaries each spring is a small fraction of what was recorded a few decades ago, and the species is classed as critically endangered. No single cause explains the decline. Weirs, sluices, dams and hydroelectric turbines stand between the sea and much of the habitat the eel once used, blocking young eels on the way up and killing silver eels on the way down. A parasitic worm that lodges in the swim bladder, brought to Europe with eels imported from East Asia, is now widespread and may leave infected animals unable to complete a long swim at depth. Pollution leaves chemical residues in the fat the eel depends on for its final journey. Glass eels are fished intensively, in part because eel farming has never managed to breed the animal through every stage of its life and so remains dependent on young eels caught in the wild. Shifts in the ocean currents that deliver the larvae may matter as much as any of these, and are the hardest of all to manage. An animal that was once so common that it was given to the poor is now the subject of urgent conservation effort across a continent.

runs.t: Every map is an argument about what matters, and the history of map-making is a history of changing purposes.

A map is not a picture of the world. It is a flat, reduced and selective statement about the world, and each of those three words conceals a problem that map-makers have spent several thousand years trying to solve. Flatness requires a method for representing a curved surface on a sheet. Reduction requires a consistent scale. Selection requires somebody to decide what is worth drawing, and that decision has always depended less on the land itself than on what the map was for.

The oldest surviving attempt at a map of the whole world is a small Babylonian clay tablet. It shows the known lands as a disc, with Babylon near the middle and a ring of water, labelled as a bitter river, drawn around the outside. Beyond that ring the tablet places regions described in writing rather than drawn to any scale. The object is not a guide to travel; it is a statement about the shape of creation and about where its centre lies, and in that respect it set a pattern that would be followed for a very long time.

Greek scholarship introduced measurement. Having accepted that the earth was a sphere, Greek geographers set about estimating its size, and the best known of these attempts used the difference between the shadows cast at noon on the same day in two Egyptian cities a known distance apart. The result was remarkably close to the modern figure. The tradition reached its height in Alexandria in the second century AD with Ptolemy, whose
Geography

was less a map than a set of instructions for making one. It listed thousands of places as pairs of numbers, a latitude and a longitude, so that a map could be reconstructed from the text alone by anyone who understood the system, and it discussed how the curved surface might be laid out on a flat page. Ptolemy also made the earth considerably too small, an error that was still being repeated more than a thousand years later and that encouraged navigators to believe Asia lay within an easy westward sail.

Ptolemy’s work was preserved and extended in the Arabic-speaking world while it was largely unknown in western Europe. Scholars there corrected his coordinates where travellers’ reports allowed; the most celebrated of their own surveys was compiled in twelfth-century Sicily for a Norman king, combining the accounts of merchants and pilgrims into a map and an accompanying description of the inhabited world. Its orientation, with south at the top, is a useful reminder that north is a convention and not a fact.

In medieval Europe the dominant form was the mappa mundi, which organised the world around a sacred centre rather than around a journey. East was placed at the top, Jerusalem at the middle, and the space between was filled with cities, rivers, scenes from scripture and the strange peoples and beasts that were believed to live at the edges of the earth. Such maps are often described as inaccurate, but accuracy of position was not what they were attempting. They were summaries of knowledge and belief, meant to be read and contemplated, and a traveller would no more have used one to find a road than a modern reader would navigate by a diagram of the solar system.

Practical navigation produced a quite different object. From the thirteenth century onwards, Mediterranean sailors used portolan charts, whose coastlines were built up from the accumulated records of voyages and are startlingly close to their true shapes. These charts show almost nothing of the interior, but they are covered by a web of straight lines radiating from compass roses placed around the sheet, allowing a navigator with a compass to lay off a course between two ports. Here, for the first time, the map was a working instrument, and its makers were tradesmen serving shipowners rather than scholars serving princes.

Ocean voyaging made the problem of flatness urgent. On a globe, a course steered at a constant compass bearing is a curve, and on an ordinary chart it cannot be drawn as a straight line. The projection published by Gerardus Mercator in the sixteenth century solved this by stretching the spacing of the parallels towards the poles by exactly the amount needed to make such a course appear straight. The price was a severe distortion of area: on a Mercator map the lands of the far north and south swell enormously, so that Greenland rivals Africa, which is in truth many times larger. The projection is therefore excellent for the single purpose for which it was designed and misleading for almost every other, which is the ordinary condition of maps.

Position at sea remained half-solved. Latitude could be found readily enough by measuring the sun or a star above the horizon, but longitude requires comparing local time with the time at a chosen reference meridian, and no clock would keep time through months of damp, rolling weather. The eventual answer, in the eighteenth century, was a marine timekeeper built to run accurately at sea. On land the same century saw governments begin systematic national surveys based on triangulation, in which a single baseline is measured on the ground with great care and a chain of triangles is then extended across the country from it by observing angles alone. These surveys were slow and costly, and they were paid for by states with military interests rather than by the sellers of maps.

Photography from the air, and later from orbit, changed the gathering of information rather than its purpose. A modern mapping agency works from imagery that is refreshed continually, and the position of any point can be fixed by satellite to within a few centimetres. Yet the final questions are the ones the Babylonian scribe faced: what to include, what to leave out, what to place at the centre and whose names to use. A digital map chooses on the user’s behalf, quietly and invisibly, and is no less a selection for being made of data.

Of all the things human beings make, buildings are among the longest-lived and the most demanding. They consume a large share of the energy used in the world, both in keeping their occupants warm, cool and lit and in the manufacture of the materials from which they are assembled. What makes this more than an engineering problem is the timescale. A car is replaced within a decade or two; an office block may still be standing in a hundred years, and decisions taken on a drawing board in a single afternoon — how deep the building is, which way its windows face, how its structure is framed — will govern its energy consumption for the whole of that life. Sustainable design is therefore less a style than an attempt to take seriously the fact that such choices cannot easily be revisited.

It is worth remembering that for most of history builders had no choice but to pay attention to climate, because they had no machinery with which to overcome it. In hot, dry regions the answer was mass: walls of stone or mud brick thick enough to absorb the heat of the day and release it slowly through the cold night, small openings, pale surfaces, and rooms arranged around a shaded courtyard. Some towns added tall shafts that caught the prevailing wind and drew it down into the rooms below. In hot, wet regions, where the nights bring little relief and mass is useless, the opposite logic applied: light construction, floors raised off the damp ground, wide overhanging eaves, and walls designed to let air pass straight through. These were not quaint local manners but solutions tested over many generations, and they were largely abandoned once cheap electricity and mechanical air-conditioning made it possible to put up a sealed glass tower in Stockholm and an almost identical one in Singapore and keep both at the same temperature by force.

Much of what is now called sustainable design is the recovery of that older intelligence, expressed in modern terms. Orientation comes first: in a cool climate the long face of a building is usually turned towards the midday sun to gather warmth, and in a hot one away from it. Shading is then sized to the geometry of the sun, since a horizontal projection that excludes high summer sunlight will admit the low winter sun beneath it. A building shallow enough in plan can be lit by daylight and ventilated by opening windows on opposite sides, or by allowing warm air to escape through a tall space and draw cooler air in behind it. None of these measures involves expensive technology, and all of them cost very little if they are settled while the plan is still being drawn. Once the frame is up, almost none of them can be added without rebuilding.

Northern Europe has pursued a different and more technical strategy, in which the building is treated as a vessel that must not leak. The envelope is wrapped in a continuous layer of insulation, junctions are detailed to avoid the paths through which heat escapes at corners and around openings, the glazing is triple, and the structure is sealed so thoroughly that its airtightness is tested before completion. A house built in this way may need almost no heating even in a hard winter. The approach has two consequences that its enthusiasts have sometimes been slow to admit. A building that admits no air by accident must be given air deliberately, so mechanical ventilation, with a device that recovers heat from the outgoing stream, becomes a necessity rather than a luxury. More seriously, a vessel designed to retain heat retains it in July as well as in January, and as summers grow hotter such buildings can become uncomfortable or even dangerous unless they are properly shaded and can be flushed with cool air at night.

As the energy used in running buildings falls, attention has shifted to the energy and emissions locked up in their construction. Cement is the difficulty. Making it requires heating limestone to a high temperature, and the chemical reaction that follows releases carbon dioxide from the rock itself, quite apart from whatever fuel is burned to provide the heat, so that concrete carries a heavy cost before a building is even occupied. Several responses are being pursued: replacing part of the cement with industrial by-products, designing structures that use less material, reclaiming steel sections from demolition for reuse, and building in timber, which holds carbon absorbed while the tree was growing. The most effective response of all is the least glamorous. Keeping an existing building and improving it avoids nearly all of these emissions, and a structure that is demolished and replaced by an efficient new one may take many decades to repay, in saved running energy, the carbon spent on its own construction.

A further and uncomfortable discovery is that buildings designed to be efficient frequently are not. Where consumption has been measured after occupation, it has often turned out to be substantially higher than the figures produced during design. The reasons are mundane: insulation installed with gaps, ventilation systems left in the wrong mode because nobody explained them to the caretaker, controls that occupants override because they are confusing, and modelling assumptions about hours of use that bear little relation to the event. Certification schemes have not always helped, because most of them award credit for features specified on paper rather than for consumption recorded in use, and a building can therefore collect an impressive rating and still perform poorly. The remedies are unexciting: commissioning the systems properly, explaining them to the people who will operate them, and publishing measured consumption year after year.

Finally, the frame of the question is widening. A house that uses little energy but stands where every journey must be made by car may be responsible for more emissions than a less efficient flat in a place where daily life can be managed on foot, so location and density belong in the calculation. So does adaptability. Buildings that survive for centuries usually do so because generous floor heights and simple plans allow them to become something else when their first purpose expires, while a structure tailored precisely to one tenant tends to be demolished when that tenant leaves. The conclusion is that sustainability in building is less a matter of the devices fixed to a roof than of unexciting decisions about where to build, what to build it from, how to shape it and whether it can be changed.
